case_study_insert.main_stem: Redbark Timber Haulage (RBH) is a partnership in the bulk timber road transport sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2008 by cousins Daniela and Rory Whitmore, the business operates a fleet of road trains hauling logs from Highfen forestry estates to sawmills across the north region, with a hierarchical structure led by senior partner Daniela. RBH plans to invest $960,000 in four double-trailer road trains, financed by $600,000 hire purchase and $360,000 partners' capital contributions. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $55 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. RBH faces a skills gap: only 9 of its 52 drivers hold the double-trailer licence needed for the new road trains.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — October 2025: The fleet completed 312 loads last month, averaging a payload of 26 tonnes per road train. Breakdowns fell from 9 to 5 this quarter. Fuel efficiency improved to 2.9 km per litre. Customer complaints dropped from 24 to 14 per month. A survey of 18 sawmill customers found 72% would switch providers for guaranteed 24-hour delivery, and 61% ask for carbon-report data with every load. A licensing audit shows 9 of 52 drivers still need double-trailer certification (off-the-job courses at the regional training depot cost $1,150 per driver; on-the-job mentoring is limited by the shortage of licence holders).

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Redbark Timber Haulage for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) Wholesale diesel prices have risen 14.7% year-on-year, sharply increasing fuel costs for long-haul fleets. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $12.20 to $13.00 per hour from April 2026, raising driver and depot staff costs. (3) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, increasing the cost of hire purchase and loan repayments.

questions.question_text: RBH plans to finance the $960,000 road train purchase with $600,000 hire purchase and $360,000 partners' capital contributions. Explain two advantages for RBH of using hire purchase instead of relying solely on partners' capital.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase lets RBH spread the $600,000 cost over several years while the four road trains generate revenue immediately, preserving Daniela and Rory Whitmore's partners' capital of $360,000 for working capital such as diesel, driver wages and maintenance across a workforce of 52. Tying up all partner funds in vehicles would leave the business exposed to the 14.7% diesel price rise and any sawmill payment delays without a cash buffer.

Point 2: Hire purchase treats the road trains as security for the finance, so RBH does not need to pledge private partner assets or dilute ownership. Because the vehicles are productive assets earning an $85 selling price on every unit hauled, the repayments can be matched against the income they create, easing cash flow and keeping the $360,000 capital contribution available as a safety cushion while the double-trailer licence bottleneck is cleared and the new fleet beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Redbark Timber Haulage and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: RBH is launching its guaranteed 24-hour double-trailer delivery service. Consider advertising in a national forestry trade magazine, direct mail to sawmill customers, or exhibiting at a forestry and logistics trade exhibition. Which should RBH choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National forestry trade magazine advertising: A placement in the sector's main title would reach hundreds of forestry estates, sawmills and timber buyers nationwide, building credibility for RBH's new double-trailer service and its carbon-report capability. It is cost-effective per reader, and 61% of sawmill customers already ask for carbon-report data with every load, so a well-placed advert can lead with that differentiator. However, print readership among actual decision-makers is limited, ads are easy to ignore, and measuring enquiry rates is weak, so many impressions will never convert to load contracts.

Direct mail to sawmill customers: RBH can mail its own base of 18 surveyed sawmill customers plus prospects, offering guaranteed 24-hour delivery — the single most cited switching trigger, named by 72% of survey respondents. Personalised, evidence-led mail is cheap, targeted and easy to track through follow-up calls, and it suits a small partnership without a marketing department. Its drawback is scale: it cannot efficiently reach new forestry regions outside RBH's existing Highfen-to-sawmill corridor, and poorly designed mailers risk being filed away unread.

Forestry and logistics trade exhibition: Exhibiting puts RBH face-to-face with estates, sawmills and timber buyers in one venue, enabling live demonstrations of road train payloads (26 tonnes average) and on-the-spot contract talks. Exhibitions build trust fast in a relationship-driven industry. However, stand fees, travel and staff time cost thousands of dollars for a partnership whose cash is committed to $960,000 of vehicles, and a single event delivers only one-off, geographically random exposure.

Recommendation: RBH should choose direct mail to sawmill customers. It speaks directly to the 72% who would switch for guaranteed 24-hour delivery, targets the exact buyers who control volume, costs a fraction of exhibition space, and produces measurable enquiry data within weeks. The trade magazine advert is rejected as untargeted and slow to convert; the exhibition is rejected as expensive and infrequent for a business that must fill four new road trains quickly; RBH can add a small magazine presence later, funded from first-contract revenues.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RBH with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of RBH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the trade magazine advert and trade exhibition are rejected.

questions.question_text: RBH faces a skills gap, with only 9 of its 52 drivers holding double-trailer licences. Explain two benefits for RBH of using bonus payments to motivate drivers to gain the new licence.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Bonus payments give drivers a direct financial reward for completing double-trailer certification, satisfying esteem and physiological needs and giving a clear incentive to book the $1,150 course promptly. Tying bonuses to licence completion links pay to the expansion RBH has invested $960,000 in, so drivers who help fill the four new road trains share in the gain rather than resenting the extra responsibility.

Point 2: Performance bonuses can be structured around the metrics sawmills care about — 24-hour delivery adherence, payload discipline and fuel efficiency at 2.9 km per litre — so licensed drivers who hit those targets earn more while RBH wins repeat contracts from the 72% of customers willing to switch for reliability. This raises output per driver, lowers the 5-breakdown rate further, and protects the $85 price and $30 contribution per unit that justify the hire purchase commitment. A faster licence pipeline also frees the four new road trains from yard inactivity, letting RBH start recovering the $960,000 outlay on the double-trailer investment immediately the trains arrive.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RBH's skills gap, expansion and customer expectations.

questions.question_text: RBH must close its double-trailer licence gap. Consider internal recruitment and promotion of existing drivers or external recruitment of licensed double-trailer drivers. Which should RBH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal recruitment and promotion: Promoting from within rewards loyal Highfen drivers, lifts morale and reinforces the hierarchical structure Daniela Whitmore runs, and internal candidates already understand RBH's routes, sawmill customers and safety culture. It is quicker and cheaper than external search, and the $1,150 licensing fee per driver is far less than external salary uplift. However, only drivers without licences are available to promote in volume (43 of 52 hold none), coaching capacity is constrained because on-the-job mentoring depends on the 9 existing licence holders, and internal promotion alone cannot widen the talent pool if demand for road trains outruns licence completion.

External recruitment of licensed drivers: Hiring certified double-trailer drivers delivers immediate capacity for the four new road trains, brings fresh techniques from other fleets, and relieves pressure on the 9 in-house mentors. Advertising, agency fees and higher starting salaries raise costs, and new hires still need route-specific induction on Highfen estates and sawmill drop-off protocols; cultural fit with a family partnership also cannot be guaranteed.

Decision: RBH should choose internal recruitment combined with targeted external hires only for stubborn gaps — prioritising existing drivers for licence training with bonuses. Internal development is cheaper, morale-boosting, and aligns with the $1,150 per driver certification budget already identified; RBH can certify its 43 unlicensed drivers in waves and cover peaks with one or two external hires. External-first recruitment is rejected as too costly, culturally risky and unnecessary given how quickly the licence courses can be completed, though RBH should revisit it if sawmill demand outstrips the licensing pipeline or absenteeism in the mentor group rises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment options with limited application to RBH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both recruitment options in the context of RBH.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of RBH with a well-justified decision covering cost, speed, morale and licence supply.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RBH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $600,000 ÷ ($85 − $55) = $600,000 ÷ $30 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $85 − $55 = $30. Answer: contribution per unit is $30.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RBH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. RBH can compare its 20,000-unit break-even output with production of 40,000 units to confirm the haulage operation is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 20,000 units, informing whether to commit to the four-road-train expansion.
2. Contribution per unit of $30 lets RBH model discount deals for sawmills, for example cutting the price to $80 would drop contribution to $25 and require volume above 24,000 units to hold the same profit, which Daniela can test against the 72% of customers willing to switch for guaranteed 24-hour delivery.
3. Contribution data helps managers check the expansion is bankable: each road train load must cover a share of the $960,000 hire purchase repayments alongside $600,000 fixed costs, so route contracts can be priced to clear those obligations before the second train order is confirmed.
4. Unit cost data ($600,000 ÷ 40,000 units + $55 = $70.00 a unit) lets managers benchmark quarterly performance, identify inefficiency behind the 5 breakdowns and 2.9 km per litre fuel figure, and renegotiate diesel and tyre contracts with suppliers while prices are rising 14.7%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $30 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 20,000 units vs 40,000-unit output; discount modelling vs $600,000 fixed costs; hire-purchase feasibility for the $960,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $70.00 for fuel and maintenance control.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RBH's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has RBH's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 24.0%
ROCE 2025 = 25.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 figures ($'000): gross profit $1,000,000 ÷ revenue $2,500,000 × 100 = 40.0%; 2025: gross profit $1,530,000 ÷ revenue $3,400,000 × 100 = 45.0%. Operating profit against revenue: 2024: $300,000 ÷ $2,500,000 × 100 = 12.0%; 2025: $510,000 ÷ $3,400,000 × 100 = 15.0%. Operating profit against capital employed: 2024: $300,000 ÷ $1,250,000 × 100 = 24.0%; 2025: $510,000 ÷ $2,040,000 × 100 = 25.0%. Cost of sales rose from $1,500,000 to $1,870,000 as volumes grew to 40,000 units, but fell from 60.0% to 55.0% of revenue, and capital employed rose sharply from $1,250,000 to $2,040,000 as the road train investment entered the balance sheet.

Evaluation: Profitability has strengthened across the board. Revenue grew 36.0% from $2,500,000 to $3,400,000, consistent with RBH producing 40,000 units a year and winning 72% of hesitant sawmill customers. Gross profit improved from 40.0% to 45.0%, indicating diesel and maintenance cost control improved even as bulk fuel prices rose 14.7% year-on-year. Operating profit improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, meaning overheads were absorbed well despite interest payable rising from $60,000 to $88,000. Operating profit against capital employed nudged up from 24.0% to 25.0%, so the enlarged asset base is still generating a stronger return — vital while $960,000 of road trains are being financed. Weaknesses: capital employed ballooned 63.2%, so most of the improvement in absolute profit depends on sustaining sawmill volumes; diesel volatility and interest rate rises to 6.0% could quickly compress the 45.0% gross figure if not hedged.

Conclusion: RBH's financial performance has improved. Gross profit (40.0% to 45.0%), operating profit against revenue (12.0% to 15.0%) and operating profit against capital employed (24.0% to 25.0%) all rose, backed by strong revenue growth. RBH should lock in these gains by fixing diesel supply contracts and hire purchase rates, and by completing double-trailer licensing quickly so the new capacity is fully loaded.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether RBH's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RBH of introducing GPS fleet tracking technology across its road train fleet.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: GPS tracking gives RBH real-time visibility of road train location, speed, idling and route adherence, enabling dispatchers to hit the guaranteed 24-hour delivery promise named by 72% of surveyed sawmill customers. It also cuts fuel waste behind the 2.9 km per litre figure, spots aggressive driving that drives maintenance costs and the 5-breakdown rate, and provides trip data that can be shared with customers asking for carbon-report data, winning new contracts.

Disadvantage: Installation and subscription fees add to fixed costs of $600,000 a year, while driver resistance is likely in a family partnership — staff may see tracking as surveillance, harming morale and worsening driver retention at a time when only 9 of 52 hold double-trailer licences. Tracking data also needs management time to interpret, and any breach of the data-monitoring expectations could create trust issues if drivers are not consulted and told exactly how the data will be used.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RBH's operations, costs and customer demands.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 14.7% diesel price rise, the 6.5% minimum wage increase to $13.00 and the base interest rate rise to 6.0% will affect RBH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Diesel price rise (14.7% year-on-year): Diesel is RBH's single largest variable cost inside the $55 a unit figure. A 14.7% rise adds roughly $5–$6 to the variable cost of every unit hauled; across 40,000 units a year that is $200,000–$240,000 a year, dragging contribution per unit from $30 toward $24–$25 and seriously weakening the case for $960,000 of new road trains unless surcharges or fuel hedging are agreed with sawmills.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $13.00 per hour): With 52 staff, mainly drivers and depot crew, a 6.5% rise adds roughly $1,700 per full-time employee a year, or about $88,000 across the workforce — significant but smaller than the diesel exposure, and partly offsettable through route productivity (40,000 units ÷ 52 staff ≈ 769 units per worker) and the bonus scheme tied to licence completion and delivery reliability.

Base interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If RBH's hire purchase or any loan is variable-rate, a 0.75 percentage point rise adds roughly $4,500 a year on $600,000 of financing, plus extra cost on the $360,000 partners' capital if it is effectively invested at opportunity cost. Interest payable is already $88,000 in 2025 per Appendix 2; a further rise has the mildest direct cash impact of the three and can be managed by fixing rates.

Conclusion: The 14.7% diesel price rise will have the greatest impact. It flows straight into every unit RBH hauls, totalling roughly $200,000–$240,000 a year, compressing the $30 contribution and the 45.0% gross figure that justifies the expansion. The minimum wage rise is second, adding around $88,000, while the interest rate rise is smallest in cash terms and manageable by fixing finance; RBH should respond with diesel hedging, fuel-linked customer surcharges and aggressive idle-time reduction in the tracked fleet.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to RBH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RBH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of RBH with a well-justified judgment that the diesel price rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
